extracted.intended_audience: Users/programmers of the Magma computer algebra system (mathematicians writing Magma code)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for defining, invoking, and structuring user-defined functions, procedures, mappings, and intrinsics in the Magma language, including syntax forms, argument semantics, scope rules, recursion, and packaging as intrinsics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer system intrinsics for serious computations
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be implemented as a function with two arguments; this is the approach taken by the intrinsic function Binomial(n, r), which should be employed for serious computations of binomial coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use system intrinsics (built-in routines) for efficient/serious computations rather than reimplementing common algorithms yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose mapping vs function by purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision whether to implement an algorithm by means of a function or a mapping depends on the purpose of the algorithm: if it expresses a mathematical relation between two structures, a mapping should be used; if the algorithm is primarily a programming routine, a function is more appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer mappings for mathematical relations (they have mathematical operations like composition and strict domain/range type-checking). Prefer functions for programming routines (may return multiple values, fewer type checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand difference between functions and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between functions and procedures is the effect they have when they are invoked. A function call returns one or more values, and therefore it is classed as an expression. By contrast, the effect of a procedure call is like the effect of several statements; it can change the values of identifiers, perform output and so on. For this reason, a procedure call in Magma forms a complete statement by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use functions when you need return values and expression semantics; use procedures when you need to change calling context, perform I/O, or have statement-like effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument evaluation and invocation semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: At invocation, the actual arguments are given as expressions, in a comma-separated list enclosed in parentheses. To perform a call Magma evaluates each of the expressions given as actual arguments to the function, and substitutes the resulting values for the corresponding formal arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that actual arguments are evaluated before entering the function/procedure and that evaluation results are passed to formals; functions' calls are expressions whose value is the return value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value vs reference arguments rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedure may have value arguments and reference arguments. In the case of an actual reference argument, the tilde must be followed by an identifier, not an arbitrary expression. Actual value arguments may be expressions, since it is their values alone which are passed to the formal arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ~identifier for reference args; reference args permit the procedure to modify caller variables. Ensure actual reference arguments are identifiers and consider whether they must be assigned prior to the call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference-argument usage patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways in which reference arguments may be used: (1) actual reference argument is expected to have a value assigned before the procedure call; it may be changed by the procedure; (2) actual reference argument may be an identifier without an assigned value; the formal should not be used until assigned and the final value is given to the actual reference argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedures appropriately according to whether the reference arg is an input-then-output or an output-only storage location. Note that pre-existing values will be destroyed if overwritten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-checking behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: System and user intrinsics have the same invocation syntax and semantics as user-defined functions and procedures, except that they perform type-checking on the arguments to category-level. Mappings perform type-checking on the argument and the return value, to see that they conform to the domain magma and range magma, whereas type-checking is only to the category level for system and user intrinsics, and non-existent for simple user-defined functions (unless specially coded by the user).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on intrinsics and mappings for stronger type safety; user-defined functions may need explicit checks if strict typing is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions/procedures are first-class objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions and procedures in Magma are first-class objects ... they may be stored in identifiers, passed as arguments to other functions or procedures, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can assign functions/procedures to identifiers, pass them as parameters, and return them — use this for higher-order programming (examples: passing Sin or a user function to trapezoid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms for user-defined functions/procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two syntactic forms for user-defined functions: a func-constructor whose left side contains the formal arguments and whose right side contains expressions for the return values; and a more traditional form consisting of the formal arguments and then a body of statements, including a return statement with expressions for the return values. The syntax for user-defined procedures is similar: a proc-constructor whose left side contains the formal arguments and whose right side contains a procedure invocation in terms of the formal arguments; and a more traditional form consisting of the formal arguments and then a body of statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use func/proc constructor for simple one-line definitions; use statement form (function ... end function / procedure ... end procedure) for multi-statement algorithms, loops, or when readability requires intermediate values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructor-form limitations for procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The constructor form of procedure expression is rather limited in its applicability because the right side of the constructor has to be a single procedure call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the proc-constructor when the procedure needs multiple statements; use statement-form procedure instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning multiple values from functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function has to return more than one value, then expressions for each return value must be given on the right side of the func-constructor, separated by commas. When this function is called, the values are returned in the same order in which they are given in the constructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comma-separated return expressions and assign them to multiple identifiers when calling; order is significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures do not return expressions; early exit
rubrics_metrics.description: Since a procedure does not have return values in the sense of a function's return values, it should not contain statements of the form 'return expression, ...'; however, it may contain lines of the form 'return;' which instruct Magma to stop executing the procedure call immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'return;' to exit early from a procedure, not to pass values back. For values, use reference arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: First textual use rule (scope of identifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any identifier which is a formal argument, or whose first appearance in the text of the function expression is for the purpose of having a value assigned to it, is local to the function. If the first time that an identifier appears is when it is referred to in an expression rather than when it is assigned, then Magma looks for its value outside the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer local identifiers; avoid using non-local identifiers unless you can guarantee their intended values. Non-local identifiers are visible but cannot be reassigned inside functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-local identifiers cannot be reassigned in function bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-local identifiers cannot be reassigned within a function body. In this, they resemble loop identifiers in for-statements. Magma sees both of these as members of the value class of identifiers, rather than as 'variable identifiers' in the sense of objects that can be varied by the user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to assign to non-local identifiers inside functions; assign to local formals or use reference args in procedures instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal value arguments are local and reassignable
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be noted that formal value arguments are local identifiers within a function body, and may be re-assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may reassign formals inside functions without affecting outside identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursion and use of $$
rubrics_metrics.description: A function or procedure is allowed to invoke itself within its own definition. The $$ sign in the above stands for the function currently being defined, in this case smallest. It is not possible to use the name smallest at this point, because within the statement body of the function expression the identifier smallest is undefined. Only after Magma has processed the whole function expression can it assign the function to smallest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recursion when appropriate and use $$ inside constructor or function body to reference the function being defined. Ensure recursion terminates for all inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure recursion terminates
rubrics_metrics.description: Recursive functions and procedures are characterized by this elegance, but they must be written with care. The user must ensure that the recursion will eventually terminate, irrespective of the values of the actual arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design base cases and decreasing measures to guarantee termination and avoid infinite recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-declaration for out-of-order and mutually recursive definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose that a function/procedure f is about to be defined which invokes a function/procedure according to the identifier g. If g has not yet been assigned a function/procedure, Magma will give an error ... To prevent this error, it is possible to type 'forward g;' before the definition of f begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forward declarations at main level to allow definitions that reference functions defined later and to support mutual recursion. The forward-declaration must occur on the main level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use integer division when divisors are known factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that the divisions are calculated using the integer division operator div, since it is known that the divisors are factors of the dividends and the results should lie in the integer ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you know division yields integer results (e.g., factorial quotients), use 'div' to keep results in integer ring and avoid introducing rationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural printing and formatting for output tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: A common use for a procedure is to print output. The following trivial example has no arguments, and always performs the same task, printing a line of sixty asterisks. A more flexible procedure would be one with two value arguments c and n that allow the procedure call to specify which character c is to be printed and the number n of such characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use procedures (statement form) to implement printing/formatting utilities; use printf for formatted output and value arguments to control behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reference arguments must be identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of an actual reference argument, the tilde must be followed by an identifier, not an arbitrary expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always pass a named variable (identifier) as a reference argument; expressions like ~(some_expr) are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mappings vs functions: return semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Note, in addition, that functions may return multiple values, whereas this is possible for mappings only in the sense of returning tuples (elements of Cartesian products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need multiple distinct return values that you want to unpack, use functions (which can return multiple values); if you prefer a single structured return, a mapping returning a tuple is appropriate.
